content.p: On 14 August 1974, three small Turkish Cypriot villages on the Famagusta road, Maratha, Santalaris and Aloda, were emptied of almost everyone who was still in them. Turkish Cypriot and Greek Cypriot sources agree on the central figure: 126 people were killed, most of them women, children and elderly people, and buried in mass graves. A Cyprus Mail column gives the youngest victim as a baby of 16 days and the oldest as a man of 95. The men of fighting age had already been taken away as prisoners weeks earlier, which left the villages almost without defenders.

The dead were found within days, and the villages have been argued over ever since. Turkish Cypriot officials and Turkish media describe the killings as a massacre by the Greek Cypriot paramilitary group EOKA B. The Greek Cypriot left-wing party AKEL uses the same description. Decades of searching, exhumation and DNA identification followed, and the funerals have continued into the autumn of 2026. The sources report no conviction of anyone.
content.h2: Three villages on the Famagusta road
content.p: The three villages lay close to Greek Cypriot villages, a few kilometres from Famagusta. According to Daily Sabah, the 1960 census recorded only Turkish Cypriots in them, and by 1973 they held 270 people: 124 in Maratha, 100 in Santalaris and 46 in Aloda.

The wider setting was the summer of 1974. On 15 July a coup against President Makarios, aimed at union with Greece, was carried out; Turkey's armed forces landed on 20 July. The relatives who later took their case to the European Court of Human Rights told the court that the coup was backed by the Greek Cypriot National Guard and that mass killings of Turkish Cypriots began when it started. That is their account, as the court records it, not a finding of the court.

The court's summary of the families' account says that on 20 July armed Greek Cypriots took villagers from Maratha to nearby Alanci, then separated the men aged 15 to 60 from the women and took the men to a military camp. The women and children were sent back. Some of the men were released in early August. Hürriyet Daily News and Daily Sabah, both Turkish outlets, say instead that the men were held as prisoners of war in Famagusta and then moved to Limassol. AKEL's account is close to this: the men went to a prison camp in Famagusta and later to Limassol, while the women, children and old people were left behind.

The Turkish Cypriot journalist Sevgül Uludağ, who spent decades collecting testimony about the missing, is the source for what the remaining villagers suffered in those weeks. According to the Hürriyet Daily News column that summarised her research, EOKA B members raped women, girls and even boys between 20 July and 14 August. Cyprus Mail's July 2026 column on her work says the same of women and girls, in her words. When news came of Turkey's second advance, the column says, the perpetrators decided to leave no witnesses. This is Uludağ's reading of motive, reported by others; no court has examined it.

The sources agree on the broad shape of the day but differ on details. The families' account to the European court says Greek Cypriots came to Maratha on 14 August, raided and looted houses, and brought the Santalaris villagers to Maratha. There, according to that account, everyone was killed after torture and buried by being run over with a bulldozer on the rubbish dump. It adds that the boys had been beheaded and that the women and girls had been raped, and that the bodies were crushed and unrecognisable. The Hürriyet column, citing Uludağ, says villagers from neighbouring villages, in particular Peristeronopigi (Alaniçi), took part, and that 89 people from Maratha and Santalaris were gathered in one field and 37 people from Aloda in another. It adds that some were buried alive, a claim attributed there to Uludağ's research, and that UN forensic examination showed some victims had been killed with sharp objects.

AKEL's account, which it dates to the immediate aftermath of 20 July, has a group of Greek Cypriots entering the villages, firing into the air and rounding up the inhabitants, who were taken by bus to the school in Peristeronopigi. It says the women, children and elderly were killed that August and put into mass graves, 89 in Maratha and 37 in Aloa. It quotes Nikos Genias, a Greek Cypriot soldier, in the party's newspaper Haravgi on 20 July 1998. Passing the three villages while retreating from the Pentadaktylos range, he said, EOKA B members were using excavators to dig holes and bury the elderly and children they had killed, and that one of them said, boasting, "We completed our job".

Who gave orders, and who took part, is not settled on the pages consulted. The Hürriyet column says the shepherd's testimony and that of the researcher Antonis Angastiniyotis suggest that at least one of the killers was a mainland Greek officer. The AKEL text speaks of EOKA B members; for the separate killing of Turkish Cypriot men at Tochni the same text names EOKA B members and Greek officers. The Greek Cypriot lawmaker Giorgos Koukoumas, in August 2026, said the attacks were the work of the Greek Cypriot far right.

The families' account says that on 15 August a villager returning to Aloda found the village deserted, with bulldozer tracks, hundreds of spent cartridge cases and EOKA B pamphlets. On 18 August soldiers and journalists visited. On 19 August, with UN observers present, a small pit was uncovered containing 37 bodies, which were handcuffed and had been run over, and whose heads had been cut off. The bodies had meshed together, making exhumation hard, and they were reburied together on 25 December 1974. Another source dates the opening of the Aloda grave to 20 August; the two dates are listed as a discrepancy here.

At Maratha, the court summary says, a young man named Safak Nihat, who with his family had hidden in barrels and a hayloft and then emerged to find the village burning and empty, was helping his uncle with sheep on 2 September. Near the rubbish dump he noticed a smell and four heaps shaped like pyramids, and he saw a child's arm sticking out of one. He ran to tell his uncle; soldiers and UN personnel came. According to that account 89 bodies were exhumed and the victims buried on 4 September. Turkish press accounts describe the discoverer as a shepherd who noticed a human hand. The court summary says the events were also reported in UN Secretary-General reports dated 27 August and 10 September 1974. Daily Sabah quotes the United Nations at the time calling the massacre "a further crime against humanity committed by the Greek and Greek Cypriot gunmen". Hürriyet Daily News says nine Turkish Cypriots who were not in the villages that day survived, according to its columnist.

AKEL's page includes the recollection of a survivor, Asiir Ahmet of Maratha, who described UN workers digging up dozens of headless and mutilated bodies, "mostly children that were covered only with garbage", some tied together with wire. He said his six brothers, his mother, his grandmother, and an aunt with her seven children were among the dead.

The 1974 burials did not separate the bodies of the dead. The Turkish Cypriot member of the Committee on Missing Persons in Cyprus, Gülden Plümer Küçük, said in early 2016 that no scientific identification had been done at the mass graves, so the victims were buried together, and that it was very important to families that they be identified and have separate graves. The Committee was set up in 1981 by the two communities with United Nations backing, and Daily Sabah says it is tasked with finding people who went missing in the conflicts of the 1960s and 1970s.

In 2015 it excavated the Maratha and Santalaris site. Küçük said 89 Turkish Cypriots' bodies had been found and that 50 had been taken out of the ground so far. At a commemoration, the Turkish Cypriot leader Mustafa Akıncı said 45 of the 89 people killed at Maratha and Santalaris were children under 16, that the remains of 86 had been exhumed the year before, and that work at Aloa was due to start by the end of that year. On that day, the remains of four identified women were buried. A Turkish Cypriot state broadcaster put the numbers differently at the 47-year mark: 88 people unearthed at Maratha-Santalaris, 75 identified and buried, and the identification of two more still continuing. Those figures differ from Akıncı's, and the pages do not explain why.

The burials followed one another. AKEL reported the funeral of 15 victims in December 2018. In December 2020 fourteen children, seven girls and seven boys, whose identities had been confirmed by DNA, were buried, the youngest four months old and the oldest 15, according to Daily Sabah. After 47 years of waiting, eleven children aged from 3 to 17 were buried in individual graves at a state ceremony. On a Friday evening in September 2026 a funeral was held for 15 more victims, nine of them children, at the Aloa cemetery. The Cyprus Mail listed them by name and age, from 56-year-old Ayse Hasan to 40-day-old Seldem Ali Osman. The Turkish Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhurman spoke at the opening of a museum built to document the massacres, and said that those who murdered the villagers "murdered humanity".

Hürriyet's columnist wrote in 2015 that not one Greek Cypriot had been charged. In August 2026 Greek Cypriot politicians said much the same: the former foreign minister Erato Kozakou-Marcoullis said nobody on the Greek Cypriot side had been punished for the deaths and urged both communities to acknowledge the truth and apologise to each other, and Koukoumas said most of those responsible had never been brought to justice. Hürriyet Daily News reports that the posts drew support from some Greek Cypriots and politicians.

The only court record in the sources is the European Court of Human Rights. A group of 63 Turkish Cypriot relatives of the 126 dead applied in February 2012, represented by a Nicosia lawyer, Y. Renda. They said that in 2009 an elderly Greek Cypriot who wanted to clear his conscience had given some of them the names of the perpetrators, and that most were people they had known as neighbours before 1974. They gave the Attorney General a petition naming 30 men on 9 December 2009. The Cypriot government told the court that its Attorney General had ordered a police investigation on 23 September 2009, after a Turkish Cypriot newspaper article, with 15 people named in it at the centre.

The government's account of what followed: of the names, four had been listed twice, one person could not be identified, one had moved abroad with no known address, and eleven were dead. Police took statements from the rest. The families said four of the suspects' statements, submitted in the Cypriot court proceedings, said essentially that they had left the area because of the fighting and did not know who had done it, and complained that the authorities had looked for 15 of their 30 names. By July 2013 the Attorney General said the investigation was continuing.

The European judges followed two earlier decisions on similar complaints and rejected the application as premature and manifestly ill-founded. The Court said it appeared that an investigation was underway and that considerable steps had been taken to gather evidence. It added that, as in the earlier cases, the authorities must take reasonable steps and keep families informed. The decision did not decide who was guilty. The sources give no later prosecution.

How the event is remembered differs by community and by party. The Greek Cypriot left-wing party AKEL calls the killings among the most shameful acts in the country's history and says many Greek Cypriots know little about them. It also says a cycle of retaliation followed, including killings of Greek Cypriot civilians by Turkish Cypriot extremists, and that Turkish officials use these crimes as propaganda to justify the Turkish army's presence. In 2015 Hürriyet's columnist, by contrast, treated the killings as proof of a Greek Cypriot denial mentality. A Turkish-language newspaper links the massacre to Turkey's second operation: it writes that the massacre was cited by the Turkish armed forces as one of the reasons for the operation's second phase.

The 2026 funeral speeches showed the argument still running. Erhurman criticised a European Parliament budget amendment, tabled by the Greek Cypriot European Parliament member Michalis Hadjipantela, that asked for a monument to those missing because of the 1974 invasion alone. He also called a report on sexual violence that documented only Greek Cypriot victims biased. A Cyprus Mail column the same summer made a related complaint, that an AKEL-backed amendment recognising Turkish Cypriot victims had been rejected, while also noting that perpetrators on both sides of the island were often local men from neighbouring villages.
